item.title: Children & Teens (Under 18)
item.description:
Children and teenagers are frequent users of online gaming, video sharing, messaging, and social networks. Because of their active digital presence and relative inexperience, they face unique cyber risks often concealed within entertainment or social platforms.

Common Threats

  • Online Gaming Scams and Fake Cheat Codes: Offers of free gaming currency, skins, or cheats often lead to credential theft or malware. Learn more about Unexpected Money & Prize Scams and Gambling Scams.
  • Social Media Grooming and Deception: Strangers posing as peers or trusted individuals to extract personal information or private photographs. Explore Social Media Scams and Phishing.
  • Sextortion and Image-Based Blackmail: Coercion tactics that exploit private media to demand money or further compromises. See Social Media Scams and Identity Theft & Fraud.
  • Malicious Apps and APKs Shared via Messaging: Unofficial game modifications and download links shared in chat groups that install spyware or trackers. Learn how to identify Ransomware & Malware and Scam Text Messages.
  • Gambling-Themed and Too-Good-To-Be-True Offers: Loot boxes, skin betting, and free-gift claims designed to extract card details. Review Gambling Scams and Unexpected Money Scams.

Avoidance Steps

  • Use Parental Controls and Supervised Accounts: Set up device-level screen time, content filters, and store purchase restrictions.
  • Guard Personal Information: Never share your real name, school, home address, phone number, or live location in gaming handles or public profiles.
  • Install from Official Stores Only: Avoid sideloading APK files or downloading software from chat links and unverified websites.
  • Maintain Open Communication: Talk with parents, guardians, or trusted adults if an online contact makes you feel uncomfortable, frightened, or pressured.
  • Enable Privacy Settings: Ensure social media accounts and gaming profiles are restricted to approved friends and contacts.

Universal Red Flags

  • Demands for secrecy or urging you not to tell parents or teachers.
  • Unsolicited links offering free items, currency, or special privileges.
  • Pressure to act immediately or threats of exposure.
  • Requests to move conversations away from moderated game platforms to unmonitored private messaging apps.

item.title: Young Adults (18–34)
item.description:
Young adults, including Gen Z and younger Millennials, are digital natives who conduct the majority of their shopping, banking, employment searches, and social interactions online. Despite their digital fluency, surveys consistently show younger adults report frequent financial losses to social-media-originated scams, employment fraud, and speculative investment schemes.

Common Threats

  • Social-Media-Originated Scams: Deceptive advertisements, sponsored influencer promotions, and fake brand giveaways designed to collect payment credentials or personal data. Learn more about Social Media Scams, Online Sales Scams, and Unexpected Money Scams.
  • Speculative Investment and Crypto Schemes: High-yield investment programs, fake trading bots, and social-media tips promising unrealistic returns with zero risk. Read about Investment Scams.
  • Job and Employment Scams: Work-from-home offers, task scams, and fake recruitment where applicants are asked to pay upfront onboarding fees, buy equipment, or process fraudulent payments. Review Job Scams.
  • Deepfake Videos and Audio Cloning: Artificial intelligence tools used to generate synthetic videos or clone voices of colleagues, executives, or friends asking for urgent assistance. Learn about AI-Powered Scams and Spoof Calls and Fake Caller IDs.
  • Peer-to-Peer Payment Fraud and Money Muling: Solicitations to move funds through personal bank accounts, payment apps, or cryptocurrency wallets under the guise of casual work. Explore Money Mule Scams.
  • Phishing and Account Takeovers: Credential harvesting via fake login portals, malicious links, and SIM hijacking. See Phishing, Phone Porting and SIM Swap Scams, and Identity Theft and Identity Fraud.

Avoidance Steps

  • Pause and Verify: Stop before clicking on sponsored social media deals, urgent direct messages, or too-good-to-be-true investment offers.
  • Verify Employment Opportunities: Thoroughly research companies through independent corporate directories; never send money for equipment, background checks, or activation.
  • Treat Cloned Media with Skepticism: If a friend or coworker contacts you via voice or video asking for urgent money transfers, verify by calling them directly on their known, verified phone number.
  • Never Move Money for Others: Refuse any proposal to receive and transfer funds on behalf of an employer, online acquaintance, or acquaintance. Money muling is a serious legal offense.
  • Secure Accounts with Multi-Factor Authentication: Use dedicated authenticator apps or hardware keys instead of SMS wherever possible, and maintain unique passwords using a password manager.

Universal Red Flags

  • Fast-money guarantees or high returns with “zero risk.”
  • Employers who hire without an interview and require payments from you.
  • Urgent requests from contacts claiming their phone is broken or demanding payments through gift cards or crypto.
  • Requests to move conversations to encrypted chat apps immediately after initial contact.

item.title: Middle-Aged Adults (35–54)
item.description:
Middle-aged adults often manage significant financial responsibilities, including home loans, children’s education, retirement investments, and workplace procurement. Cybercriminals frequently target this age group with sophisticated blended threats that cross the boundary between personal life and professional obligations.

Common Threats

  • Investment and Stock/Crypto Schemes: Sophisticated fraudulent investment websites, false trading advisers, and pre-IPO stock opportunities targeting retirement portfolios and savings. Learn more about Investment Scams.
  • Online Shopping and Marketplace Fraud: Bogus sellers, counterfeit merchant storefronts, and overpayment scams when selling personal items or vehicles online. Review Online Sales Scams and Credit Card Fraud.
  • Phishing and Vishing in Professional Contexts: Targeted emails and phone calls that mimic banks, utility companies, tax departments, or suppliers requesting credential verification. See Phishing, Scam Calls and Spam Calls, and Email Scams.
  • Business Email Compromise and Intercepted Invoices: Hacked or spoofed supplier emails altering banking details for large payments, home settlements, or contractors. Explore Business Email Compromise.
  • Account Takeovers and Identity Fraud: Theft of personal details used to apply for credit cards, take out loans, or hijack telecommunication accounts. See Identity Theft and Identity Fraud and Phone Porting and SIM Swap Scams.
  • Hybrid Technical Attacks: QR code traps, malicious attachments, and remote software prompts disguised as technical support or document readers. Explore Remote Access Scams, Quishing and QR Code Scams, and Ransomware.

Avoidance Steps

  • Verify Financial Advisers and Investments: Cross-reference any financial adviser, broker, or investment entity with official government registers before committing funds.
  • Navigate Directly to Services: Type official URLs directly into your browser or use verified mobile apps rather than following links in emails or SMS notifications.
  • Confirm Invoices and Bank Detail Changes: Always call the vendor, builder, or solicitor on an independently verified telephone number before acting on updated bank account numbers.
  • Monitor Accounts and Review Credit Reports: Regularly examine bank and credit card statements, enable transaction alerts, and check credit scores for unexpected inquiries.
  • Promote Household Cyber Hygiene: Ensure devices across the home are kept updated and discuss common scam tactics with children, teens, and aging parents.

Universal Red Flags

  • Last-minute changes to payment instructions or bank accounts for high-value transactions.
  • Urgent claims of outstanding tax penalties, toll road fines, or package delivery failures requiring immediate payment.
  • High-pressure sales tactics that attempt to bypass your usual verification or consultation processes.
  • Requests to install remote diagnostic or desktop-sharing software to resolve an alleged problem.

item.title: Older Adults (55+)
item.description:
Older adults and senior citizens are heavily targeted by cybercriminals who exploit trust, authority, fear, and unfamiliarity with rapidly evolving digital interfaces. Fraudulent schemes targeting this demographic often involve direct phone contact, aggressive pressure, and substantial financial losses.

Common Threats

  • Tech-Support and Remote Access Scams: Alarming browser pop-ups or phone calls claiming a computer is infected with viruses, directing the victim to grant remote access and pay for fake diagnostic software. Learn more about Remote Access Scams.
  • Impersonation and “Digital Arrest” Scams: Criminals posing as law enforcement officers, police, central investigative agencies, tax authorities, or judges. They intimidate victims through video calls with false allegations of money laundering or narcotics, threatening immediate “digital arrest” unless money is transferred to “verification” accounts. Review Bank Impersonation Scams, Spoof Calls and Fake Caller IDs, and Scam Calls and Spam Calls.
  • Government, Tax, and Pension Rebates: Deceptive messages claiming unclaimed refunds, pension bonuses, or utility rebates that require sharing banking credentials or paying an upfront fee. See Unexpected Money & Tax Refund Scams and Scam Text Messages.
  • Family Emergency and Romance Scams: Deceptive messages claiming a child or grandchild has lost their phone and urgently needs money for a bill or legal trouble (such as the “Hi Mum/Dad” scam), or prolonged emotional manipulation by online suitors. Explore Scam Text Messages and Social Media Scams.
  • Charity and Healthcare Fraud: Fabricated humanitarian appeals and fraudulent healthcare supplements targeting seniors. Review Charity Scams.
  • Banking and Payment Card Fraud: Unauthorised debits and deceptive callers requesting one-time passcodes under the guise of account protection. See Credit Card Fraud.

Avoidance Steps

  • Recognize That “Digital Arrest” Is Fake: Law enforcement agencies, police, tax departments, and courts never arrest individuals over video calls, demand immediate wire transfers, or require payments via UPI, gift cards, or cryptocurrency. Hang up immediately.
  • Never Grant Remote Access: Do not allow unexpected callers or pop-up prompts to install remote management software (such as AnyDesk or TeamViewer) on your device.
  • Ignore Infection Pop-Ups: Pop-up alerts warning of viruses with a phone number to call are fraudulent. Close the browser window or restart your device.
  • Consult Family Before Transferring Funds: Always pause and discuss unexpected requests for money, investment opportunities, or legal crises with trusted family members or friends.
  • Establish Family Code Words: Use a simple family verification word or call back on the original known number when receiving messages claiming to be a child or grandchild with a new phone.
  • Use Call Screening and Spam Protection: Enable carrier call-filtering features and let unknown callers go to voicemail.

Universal Red Flags

  • Aggressive callers who shout, threaten arrest, or demand that you stay on a video call while visiting a bank.
  • Requests for payment through unusual channels like cryptocurrency, gift cards, or immediate wire transfers to personal accounts.
  • Anyone instructing you to keep a transaction secret from your family, bank branch staff, or friends.
  • Demands for your bank PIN, password, or one-time security codes over the phone or SMS.
